global.title: Web project conventions
global.tagline: Give your agent the habits of a careful senior web developer, from the first commit.
global.summary: Starting instructions for any website or web app: semantic HTML, WCAG 2.1 AA, a colour system with a clear visual hierarchy, tokenized fluid CSS, readable naming, navigation, forms, loading states, AI discoverability and secure server defaults.
highlights: Semantic HTML and WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility on every component
A colour system that sets visual hierarchy: brand, accent, elevation and traffic-light status colours
Colours, font sizes and every spacing value as :root tokens, with layouts arranged by the parent
Names a developer understands at first sight, by value, state and goal
Navigation where users always know where they are and what comes next
Forms with inline, as-you-type guidance, and sign-in/sign-up tabs that accept browser-suggested passwords
AI discoverability: server-rendered content, a generated llms.txt, crawler rules and JSON-LD
Skeletons, empty and error states for every async operation
Server-side validation, authorization and correct HTTP status codes, with no leaked internals
Branded 404, safe redirects and unique page titles
usageSteps: Download `global.md`. It's free.
Save it in your project's root, then add the line `@global.md` to your `CLAUDE.md` so Claude Code loads it in every session. With no `CLAUDE.md` yet, rename the file to `CLAUDE.md` instead.
Work as usual. The agent applies the conventions to every file it creates or changes, and follows your codebase where it already does things differently.
Add a framework-specific file, such as `nextjs-structure.md`, on top of it for project structure.

nextjs-structure.title: Next.js project structure
nextjs-structure.tagline: Stop asking where the file goes. Your agent already knows.
nextjs-structure.summary: Where every file goes in a Next.js App Router project: src/ layout, routes-only app/, component folders, server-only code, public/ assets, aliases, titles and route protection.
highlights: A complete src/ tree showing where every kind of file belongs
app/ holds routes only, with the home page in a (homepage) route group
Component folders per route, per feature and global/, with no loose files
Server-only code in src/server/, guarded with server-only imports
Static files in public/; paid or private files served through an access-checked route
@/* imports with no barrel files, and one title template for every page
proxy.ts for redirects, with real permission checks in every handler
usageSteps: Buy and download `nextjs-structure.md`.
Save it in your project's root, then add the line `@nextjs-structure.md` to your `CLAUDE.md` so Claude Code loads it in every session.
On a new project, ask the agent to scaffold it following the file. On an existing one, it keeps your current structure where it differs and tells you about the difference.
Let the agent keep the structure section of your `CLAUDE.md` current as it adds routes and folders.

dev-tools-advisor.title: Dev tools and stack advisor
dev-tools-advisor.tagline: Let your agent research the tools that fit your project, not the ones in fashion.
dev-tools-advisor.summary: Recommends a linter, formatter, test runner, package manager, framework or library from your project and your setup: it detects your environment, researches current docs and respects the tools you already chose.
highlights: Detects your OS, editor, version manager and stack before recommending anything
Asks only what it can't read from the repo, and offers to save your setup so other projects don't ask again
Researches each tool's current docs and maintenance instead of recommending from memory
Compares by compatibility, simplicity, editor integration and migration cost
One recommendation and one alternative, with exact commands for your shell and package manager
Respects your decisions: if you already chose a tool, it sets it up well instead of arguing
Records every decision in the project's instructions so it isn't reopened
usageSteps: Download `dev-tools-advisor.md`. It's free.

Save it in your project's root and reference it from the instruction file your agent reads (for example the line `@dev-tools-advisor.md` in `CLAUDE.md`, or its content in `AGENTS.md` or your Cursor rules).

Run it right away by sending your agent a prompt. In a project in progress: `Follow dev-tools-advisor.md and review the tools in this project.` In an empty folder: `Follow dev-tools-advisor.md and recommend a stack for a booking web app.` The agent detects your setup and asks only for what's missing.
From then on, ask about a single tool whenever you need it (for example "ESLint and Prettier, or Biome?"), or start a new project, and the agent applies the advisor on its own.
Approve the recommendation. The agent installs it, runs it once to confirm it works, and records the decision.

commit-attribution.title: Commit messages without AI attribution
commit-attribution.tagline: Your history describes the change, not the tool that helped write it.
commit-attribution.summary: Keeps commit messages, pull request texts and release notes free of AI credits: no Co-Authored-By trailers, no generated-with lines, no session links. Includes how to write a clear message and an optional commit-msg hook that enforces it.
highlights: Removes assistant trailers, generated-with lines and session links from commits and pull requests
Strips lines that an agent's template, a generator or a hook injects before the commit is created
Keeps what belongs: real co-authors, sign-offs and issue references
Subject and body rules: imperative mood, about 50 characters, the why in the body
Fixes an unpushed commit with amend or reword, and leaves pushed history to you
An optional commit-msg hook that rejects attribution lines for the whole team
Defers to your project's policy if it asks for AI assistance to be disclosed
usageSteps: Download `commit-attribution.md`. It's free.

Save it in your project's root and reference it from the instruction file your agent reads (for example the line `@commit-attribution.md` in `CLAUDE.md`, or its content in `AGENTS.md` or your Cursor rules).
Commit as usual. The agent writes the message from the change and removes any attribution line before creating the commit.
To enforce it for everyone, copy the optional `commit-msg` hook from section 5 into your repository.

authentication-forms.title: Authentication forms
authentication-forms.tagline: Sign-in and sign-up forms that guide users as they type, and accept the password their browser suggests.
authentication-forms.summary: How to build sign-in, sign-up and password forms: one tabbed card instead of a link at the bottom, validation as the user types, guidance under each field, a live example that turns green as it is met, and password rules that accept browser-generated passwords.
highlights: Sign-in and sign-up as tabs in one card, labelled by who the user is, with full keyboard support
Each field validated as the user types, showing only what is still missing
A live example line, such as name@domain.com, whose chunks turn green as they are met
Border and focus ring mark valid and invalid fields, without recolouring the text
Password rules that accept what Chrome, Safari and password managers generate
Show, copy and generate controls that appear when the user needs them
A submit button that stays enabled and focuses the first wrong field
The same rules defined once for the client and the server
usageSteps: Download `authentication-forms.md`. It's free.

modals.title: Modals
modals.tagline: Know when a modal can be dismissed, and make every one behave the same.
modals.summary: Two kinds of modal, chosen by whether closing it is a meaningful decision: non-dismissible ones close only through an action-named button, dismissible ones close three ways. Plus shared styling, native dialog behaviour and accessibility.
highlights: One question picks the kind: is closing this modal a meaningful decision?
Non-dismissible modals close only through action-named buttons, with Cancel always present
Dismissible modals close with an outside click, Escape and a floating X
Shared title, input, close and action classes, defined once instead of per modal
Built on the native dialog element, with focus moved in and returned to the trigger
A busy state on the action button while the request is in flight
Calm motion for users who prefer reduced motion

loading-states.title: Loading states
loading-states.tagline: No frozen screens: every async operation shows what is happening and what went wrong.
loading-states.summary: What the interface shows while something asynchronous happens, and when it fails or comes back empty: an explicit status, skeletons that match the content, busy buttons, no flicker on fast responses and accessible announcements.
highlights: An explicit idle, loading, success or error status, always cleared in a finally
Skeletons that mirror the final layout, so the page doesn't jump when data arrives
Buttons that show their busy state, stay disabled in flight and keep their width
Loaders delayed and held a minimum time, so fast responses don't flicker
Empty and error states for every view, with a retry action
Announced to assistive technology and calm under reduced motion
Spinners and skeletons built once as reusable components

error-handling-and-http-status.title: Error handling and HTTP status codes
error-handling-and-http-status.tagline: Safe messages for users, the right status for clients, and the details only in your logs.
error-handling-and-http-status.summary: How a server answers when something goes wrong and how a client reads it: no leaked internals, errors translated into messages in the user's terms, the correct HTTP status code, a stable error body and a request ID for support.
highlights: No database, framework or stack-trace detail ever reaches the client
Known failures mapped to the right status and a message in the user's terms
A generic 500 with a request ID for everything unexpected
Full technical errors logged on the server, without secrets
No failure inside a 200 body, and a status code chosen deliberately
One stable error body with field-level messages and a request ID
Client handling of 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429 and 5xx

ai-discoverability-geo.title: AI discoverability
ai-discoverability-geo.tagline: Make your site easy for AI assistants to find, read and quote.
ai-discoverability-geo.summary: How to make a public website discoverable by AI assistants: server-rendered content, a generated llms.txt, deliberate crawler rules in robots.txt, sitemap and canonical basics, JSON-LD and writing that can be quoted.

A generated /llms.txt in the llmstxt.org format that never goes stale
Search, user-fetch and training crawlers configured on purpose in robots.txt
Sitemap, canonical URLs, unique titles and descriptions, and Open Graph tags
JSON-LD for the home page and for each page type, matching the visible text
Answer-first headings and specific facts that models can quote

security-validation-authorization.title: Server security: validation and authorization
security-validation-authorization.tagline: Never trust the client: check every input and every permission on the server.
security-validation-authorization.summary: How to protect server code that handles input, accounts and data: an OWASP check, schema validation of everything that crosses the boundary, authority taken only from the verified session, and authorization of the specific resource on every path.
highlights: An OWASP Top 10 check before touching input, auth, sessions, uploads or data access
Server-side validation with a schema shared by client and server, rejecting unknown fields
Roles, prices and ownership derived on the server, never taken from the request
A reusable guard at the top of every handler, deny by default
Ownership and role checked on each resource, which prevents IDOR
Every path covered: all methods, bulk operations, downloads and subscriptions
Secrets kept out of the repository and the client bundle

routing-and-404.summary: How to name routes, ship a branded 404 with a real 404 status, redirect only to safe internal paths, kick users out of privileged pages when they log out and enforce the same rules on the server.

Route guards that react to logout and use replace, so Back can't return to a protected page
Privileged data cleared from client state when the session ends
The server re-checks authentication and role, answering 401 or 403
